Mass Extinction: Lessons from Chernobyl.

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With the world in the grip of its sixth mass extinction, what can we learn from nature's resurgence in one of the most toxic places on the planet?

Unique Selling Point:
In a South African television first, Carte Blanche ventures into one of the most contaminated places in the world to investigate how nature is reclaiming what humans took away. In spite of life-threatening ionising radiation, Chernobyl's wildlife is thriving. We'll venture into the Exclusion Zone and hear from experts who are trying to understand why.

Summary:
We're in the midst of the Sixth Mass Extinction. Animals and insects are dying out at rates up to 1000 times the natural average. Unlike previous mass extinction events, this one is being driven by humans through the destruction of natural habitats, the use of pesticides, poaching and a myriad other unsustainable behaviours. The implications are, potentially, catastrophic.

But, a 2600 square kilometre area of forest in northern Ukraine provides a blunt but valuable lesson about our relationship with the remaining biosphere.

The massive Exclusion Zone set up around the Chernobyl nuclear facility shortly after the calamitous explosion in its fourth reactor in 1986 has successfully limited human activity in the area. And for good reason: it remains, along with Fukushima in Japan, the most contaminated place on the face of the planet. Extended exposure to ionising radiation in its most toxic areas can lead to serious health issues and death. But, it has also had an unexpected and ironic impact. Animals, birds, fish and flora are thriving. Nature has, over the past three decades, reclaimed the abandoned buildings and quiet roads. Wolves, antelope, moose and bears have returned in numbers not seen since the area was cleared and colonised by humans. The lesson is stark: take man out of the equation, and nature's resilience ensures not just its survival but its proliferation.

While not a scientific or even particularly sophisticated argument, there does appear a stark lesson: if you want to ensure nature's survival, simply leave it alone.

Script:


UPSOUND (53:19 of IPBES briefing) “The question is what will the world look like in 2050? It is our choice. It is purely our choice…

VO: These people came together in May this year to hear about an unfolding crisis.
Media briefing GVs incl, wide of top table into black and white free stills of barren landscapes

VO: Hundreds of scientists spent three years analyzing more than 15 thousand publications and arrived at an alarming conclusion: we’re in trouble. Up to a million animal and plant species are at risk of vanishing forever in what’s known as a mass extinction. There have been others, but what makes this one different is that this time, it’s our fault.

UPSOUND from UN Media Briefing into GVS

VO: The experts warned that human activity like factory farming and overfishing are causing extinction rates to accelerate, describing the loss of life as unprecedented. But, when you consider what’s at stake, the mood was upbeat…

UPSOUND: (1:02:01 of IPBES briefing) “We are a single inter-connected web of life…” into wide

VO:… and a little defiant.

UPSOUND: (1:02:34 of IPBES briefing) “You have to claim your birth right to have a fulfilling life, deeply connected with the fabric of life which is healthy and in working order.”

VO: But how do we do that? Well, sometimes you find answers in unlikely places. So, we touched base with an expert who could help point the way.

Upsound: Hello Prof, could you drop your screen slightly

VO: This is Prof Nick Beresford. He doesn’t say any more than is necessary but as a respected voice on the impacts of radiation on the natural environment, what he does say is taken seriously.

John Question (Beresford listening): How many times have you been to the exclusion zone?

ITV: Nick Beresford [23:24 – 23:30] Oh, I’ve lost count now… uhm, about twenty-ish

John (Beresford listening): 20 times. As many as that…

ITV: Nick Beresford (23:33 – 23:35) Maybe more now, around about that.

VO: That’s more than 20 visits to one of the most contaminated places on the planet. Thousands of square kms of mostly abandoned buildings, woodland and small areas of savannah straddling the border between Ukraine and Belarus, an Exclusion Zone around the site of history’s worst ever nuclear accident: Chernobyl. The professor is one of those who believes it holds clues as to how, what the experts in Paris called the “fabric of life”, might be rejuvenated. We decided to have a look for ourselves.

VO: That’s a Geiger counter, warning us of increasing radiation levels in the area we’re driving through. This landscape is a patchwork of varying levels of contamination - average in places, extremely hazardous in others. Knowing one from the other is important.

VO: At the time of the accident, Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union and Moscow had grand plans for Chernobyl – to build a mega-nuclear facility. But, 33 years ago, there was an explosion in one of its reactors.

Upsound Russian tv announcement and more archive

Link Reactor 4 (1): The infamous reactor 4. In 1986 a combination of human error and technical shortcomings resulted in a tragedy of biblical proportions. Its consequences were felt not only here in the Ukraine but in neighbouring Belarus and as far away as Germany, Sweden and even Britain.

ITV David Nicholls [00:48:13] STRAP: “Former Chief Nuclear Officer, Eskom” a technology or anything you do, if it is not governed appropriately, you are into major trouble.

VO: David Nicholls, is the now retired Chief Nuclear Officer at Eskom. He argues that the Chernobyl disaster was about people rather than technology.

ITV David Nicholls [00:01:06] the reactor got to a point of nuclear balance where it basically ended up acting with an incredibly high rate of power. So, it went in a very short time up to about 30000 times its design power level. And basically, that could blow up.

VO: The explosion released 400 times more radiation than the bombing of Hiroshima. Some estimates say the disaster will eventually claim 4000 lives, other figures are far higher - consensus another of Chernobyl’s casualties. (PAUSE)

VO: In the immediate aftermath, the impacts should have been more obvious, not least for the nearby town of Pripyat. It was home to thousands of power plant workers and their families.
Drone and ground footage of abandoned buildings (NB town shots on Disk 1 aren’t from Pripyat)

VO: But, the decision to get its residents to safety was a long-time coming.
Pripyat 1: Bizarrely, considering 50 lives hinged on the decision, Pripyat was only evacuated 36 hours after the disaster. But when it eventually got underway on the 27th of April, it took just 3 hours to empty the town.

VO: Three decades later, Pripyat is a town frozen in time. It stands as a monument to Soviet ambition and a memorial to its failures: dozens of gas masks at a local school a sign that possible tragedy had at least been considered. The fun fair, a place for young families to build memories, now throbbing with radioactivity. It’s desolate and eerie but – ironically – also a place of rebirth.

Pripyat 2 Pripyat was a tailor-made, model Soviet town. It had 15 kindergartens, 5 schools, 2 swimming pools and housed 50 thousand people. But now, more than 30 years later, all of that is being consumed by nature. And, given where we are in human history, some people are saying there are important lessons in that.

VO: One of those people is Denis Vishnevsky. He’s an 18-year veteran of the exclusion zone – a dedicated zoologist monitoring the impacts of the Chernobyl disaster on the natural environment.

VO: Just how dedicated is demonstrated by something deemed important enough to pause our interview for. Here, in the overgrown remnants of Chernobyl’s cooling ponds, a sighting of swans is worth the interruption.

Upsound with Denys looking through binos

VO: Like hundreds of other species, the Swans appear to be flourishing in an area that – three decades earlier – they tended to avoid.

ITV: Denis Vishnevsky [04:42:24] STRAP “Chernobyl Ecology Centre” Why? Because of high levels of agricultural transformation to the territory plus urbanization. They built a new town with the infrastructure (…) roads. Plus, they built Chernobyl nuclear power plant. But after the accident everything change(d).

Wetland: In 1988, two years after the accident, this entire area was declared a nature reserve. Sure, it’s a nature reserve unlike any other but it’s still a significant size even by South African standards. If you include the area in neighbouring Belarus, 4600 square kilometres.

VO: That’s close to three times the size of the Jo’burg metro.

ITV: Nick Beresford [09:10] STRAP “Radio Ecologist: Centre for Ecology and Hydrology” It’s 4600km for the exclusion zone, but if you look at a map it actually borders other nature reserves, so as a total I guess it’s the largest nature reserve in Europe [08:52) We’ve had cameras over quite a lot of the area, so I think we’ve got a good idea of what the wildlife levels are as a whole.

VO: And somehow, in this place of lonely roads, abandoned buildings and rusting freshwater ports what might be considered mundane anywhere else becomes… well, quite spectacular.

VO: These are rare Przwalski (Shuh-VAL-skee) horses, extremely rare, their numbers are not significant, but they’re here, fighting on.

VO: And Professor Beresford’s motion cameras, installed across the Exclusion Zone, provide more evidence of arguably the most remarkable consequence of this man-made catastrophe: wildlife is thriving: more horses, Lynx, Wolf, Wild Boar. The young, the old, the curious. And none appear to be suffering the effects of radiation.

ITV: Nick Beresford (05:08) On the whole, from what you can see, yes they look quite healthy and in some instances we know they’re having a long life

John: Does that surprise you?

ITV: Nick Beresford (05:17) Uh, no, it doesn’t necessarily mean there no effects of radiation either.

VO: Research on the impacts of this toxic environment is continuing. But if there have been severe mutations, nature has likely found its own solutions.

ITV Denis Vishnevsky [04:57:15] When I catch a mouse or fish from (the) cooling pond, what (do) we get(?)We get winners. Winners (are) animals that (lose both) grow up in this ecological situation. If (an animal has two heads) it’s a big problem, a big problem for a long life maybe. We can't observe this animal because in natural situations it’s just eliminated very fast.

VO: Ironically, studies looking into the effects of radiation on plants and animals arrived at conclusions that reveal more about us than they do about the wildlife.

ITV: David Nicholl [00:35:51] every study they looked at, every data they looked at was dwarfed by the impact of removing human beings from the environment. So that dwarfed any other change that taking human beings out of the environment did more to change more positive good for the wildlife

VO: So, it might not be particularly scientific, but there is something to learn from this place.

John: Does Chernobyl provide a lesson for humankind?

Prof Nick Beresford (12:18): Undoubtedly, we’ve actually got a proposal in at the moment looking at rewilding. Rewilding is a big issue nowadays…

John: Anything blunter than that, Prof?

Prof Nick Beresford (12:48): Well, a consequence of the accident was to remove the biggest stressor on wildlife: people.

VO: And that is arguably Chernobyl’s most profound lesson… at least when it comes to its impact on nature: the biggest threat isn’t radiation; it’s us.

Pripyat 3 Perhaps the best thing that can be said about Chernobyl is that it had honourable intentions – to provide people with electricity. Accidents are one thing but, what is less forgivable, is when the damage we cause is done on purpose.

VO: Over the years Carte Blanche has seen first-hand the deliberate destruction of the natural environment. (PAUSE) So, whether by accident or design, perhaps we shouldn’t be surprised that we’ve now reached a tipping point.

VO: And by the time we made our final pass through Chernobyl’s radiation detectors it was clear that at least part of the solution is not only providing the space for nature to flourish but making a concerted effort to just stay away.

Ends.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With the world in the grip of its sixth mass extinction, what can we learn from nature's resurgence in one of the most toxic places on the planet?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In a South African television first, Carte Blanche ventures into one of the most contaminated places in the world to investigate how nature is reclaiming what humans took away. In spite of life-threatening ionising radiation, Chernobyl's wildlife is thriving. We'll venture into the Exclusion Zone and hear from experts who are trying to understand why.
metadata.Summary: We're in the midst of the Sixth Mass Extinction. Animals and insects are dying out at rates up to 1000 times the natural average. Unlike previous mass extinction events, this one is being driven by humans through the destruction of natural habitats, the use of pesticides, poaching and a myriad other unsustainable behaviours. The implications are, potentially, catastrophic. But, a 2600 square kilometre area of forest in northern Ukraine provides a blunt but valuable lesson about our relationship with the remaining biosphere. The massive Exclusion Zone set up around the Chernobyl nuclear facility shortly after the calamitous explosion in its fourth reactor in 1986 has successfully limited human activity in the area. And for good reason: it remains, along with Fukushima in Japan, the most contaminated place on the face of the planet. Extended exposure to ionising radiation in its most toxic areas can lead to serious health issues and death. But, it has also had an unexpected and ironic impact. Animals, birds, fish and flora are thriving. Nature has, over the past three decades, reclaimed the abandoned buildings and quiet roads. Wolves, antelope, moose and bears have returned in numbers not seen since the area was cleared and colonised by humans. The lesson is stark: take man out of the equation, and nature's resilience ensures not just its survival but its proliferation. While not a scientific or even particularly sophisticated argument, there does appear a stark lesson: if you want to ensure nature's survival, simply leave it alone.
